guidance:
Work only with Table 1. Use its caption and header rows to understand structure, but take data values exclusively from the table body.

1) Table title and scope
- Set `table_title` to the exact caption of Table 1.
- Ignore other tables and figures as data sources.

2) Columns and headers
- Reconstruct the full header region from left to right before creating any cells.
- Add every explicit data column header to `columns`. This includes each group/arm, timepoint, and any separate statistics columns (e.g., effect size, relative risk) that have their own header cell.
- For multi-level headers (a top label spanning several subheaders), treat only the lowest-level headers as data columns. Build each `column_label` by combining higher-level and leaf text into a single unique string, such as "Top: Leaf".
- Do not turn the top-level header alone into a column if it only groups subcolumns.
- The leftmost label column may have a heading. If it exists, include that heading in `columns`, but never create data cells for it; its content is represented via `row_group` and `row_label`.
- Every `column_label` used in any cell must appear exactly once in `columns`. Do not invent extra columns (e.g., totals) or slightly varied names for the same column.

3) Row_group vs. row_label (table body)
- Read down the first column and separate structural lines from data lines:
  • Section/category headings: usually visually distinct, often spanning multiple columns, and followed by a block of related rows.
  • Data rows: aligned with entries in one or more data columns.
- Use each section or category heading as `row_group` for all clearly subsequent data rows it governs. For those rows, the specific descriptor on the leftmost column becomes `row_label`.
- Rows that are not under any clear heading use `row_group` = null.
- If a section heading itself has values on the same line, represent that line with `row_group` equal to the heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not swap roles: `row_group` is the broader category; `row_label` is the specific item within that category.
- When the same section or item text appears multiple times, reuse the exact wording so grouping stays consistent.

4) Creating cells and capturing values
- A cell corresponds to one non-empty intersection of a data row and a data column.
- For every visible numeric or textual entry in the body of Table 1, create exactly one cell object with fields: `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, `value`.
- Copy `value` verbatim, preserving punctuation, spaces, parentheses, ranges, units, percent signs, plus/minus signs, and textual markers (including N/A-like text or dashes when they appear as values).
- Treat printed zeros as real values and include them.
- Do not create cells for blank entries and do not infer or calculate values that are not shown.

5) Avoid missing, extra, and duplicate cells
- Work row by row: for each data row, scan across all data columns and ensure that every non-empty table entry produces exactly one cell.
- Do not create cells for rows that are purely headers or section titles and have no data values.
- Do not add derived totals, combined columns, or extra subgroup values unless they are explicitly printed in the header and body as distinct cells.
- Do not move values between categories or columns; keep each value attached to the `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label` where it is printed.
- Each combination of (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) must be unique. Never emit more than one cell for the same position.

6) String consistency
- Use the table text verbatim for `table_title`, `columns`, `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label`, preserving spelling, capitalization, spacing, and symbols.
- Confirm that every `column_label` used in `cells` matches exactly one entry in `columns`, and that identical section headings are written the same way wherever they appear.

Apply these principles to any Table 1 layout, including complex multi-level headers and multiple section blocks, so that every non-empty value is captured once in the correct structured position.
